utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. I would like the record to reflect that the late start is due to technical problems. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Lisa Biersay on behalf of the Prosecution, with Ms. Muireann Dennehy, our Case Manager Indah Susanti, and our intern Ms. Khushboo Hashu Shahdadpuri. I should also inform the Trial Chamber that midway we may be switching because I think we may be finished before the first break and the next witness will be examined by Ms. Sarah Clanton, and she will be with our intern Ms. Childs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, then, Mr. Mujanovic, do you hear us? I have a still on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, given that there's a delay with this -- the call, there is one minor procedural matter with which I would like to deal before we begin. And it might be a good time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to request that the Trial Chamber allow it to use an annotated version of the annex to the indictment which the witness has marked, and he did so and signed during proofing. The Prosecution noted -- notified the Defence of its intention to use this, and the Defence has agreed to use this. This document was circulated on Friday, and the proposed 65 ter exhibit number is 6440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So you want to add it to your 65 ter list, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution would like to seek clarification that it can use that -- this proposed exhibit with this witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Anything from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It could take another ten minutes, so we will adjourn and wait further notice. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 9.23 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujanovic. Good morning, witness. Do you hear us in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I can confirm that we can hear you but we are on another location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, we didn't notice that, you know, so that's okay. Mr. Witness, could you tell us -- you -- you have protective measures so I won't ask you your name, but the Registrar will show you a -- an identification sheet, and could you please verify whether your name and date of birth are correct, without reading them out loud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I forgot to ask you, you hear me in a language you understand, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to tell you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury, should you give untruthful or false information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Dennehy, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appear to have some problems with my audio-link. Can you just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, Mr. Hadzic has the same problem. He can -- he cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You think it will work now, Ms. Dennehy?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I hope so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic will also tell us whether can he hear once the witness -- Mr. Witness, could you count to three? Mr. Witness, did you hear me? Could you please count to three, just for testing purposes? Mr. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I can hear you loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how about the witness? Mr. Witness, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are currently having problems with the B/C/S booth. Can you give us a moment. The B/C/S both does not hear anything. It's okay now. Only -- it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems to be all right now. Mr. Witness, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, did you hear this? "Da"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but I can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could I ask you to count to three loud and clear, for testing purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We still have a problem, Madam Registrar. Madam Registrar, could you -- could you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should we test again, Mr. Hadzic? Mr. Witness, could you, once more, count to three, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. We're back in business. Thank you. Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness do you recall giving a statement to the representatives of the Tribunal on the 11th of May, 2012?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now can I ask the Court Officer to turn to tab 16 of the court bundle, and can I please ask that B/C/S version of 65 ter 2792 be shown to the witness at this time but not to be broadcast, please, at -- 65 ter 2792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime, Ms. Dennehy, you could tender the identification sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Sorry, Mr. President. I hadn't realised that it hadn't been done. In that case, can I please ask that 65 ter 6445, which was the pseudonym sheet of the witness, be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2031 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recognise the document before you to be the statement that you gave to the representatives of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please look at the signatures at the bottom of the first page and tell me whether you recognise any of those signatures?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And before testifying here today, did you have an opportunity to review your statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And during that review, you identified two minor typographical errors in your statement which I would now like you to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Could I please ask the Court Officer to turn to page 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 8 of page 3, if you look at the last sentence, do you have a correction to make to the last word in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now turning to page 12 of your statement, at paragraph 45. At the third-last sentence, which begins: "Paramilitaries took away Tihomir Perkovic ...," do you have a correction to make to the last name listed in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I now ask whether you're satisfied that the information contained in your statement is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions as you were asked in 2012 when you met the representatives of the Tribunal, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2792 into evidence under seal, and in addition pursuant to the Chamber's request, the Prosecution has also prepared a publicly redacted version of the statement which bears the 65 ter 2792.1 which may also be admitted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. The first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 2792 will become Exhibit P2032 under seal. And 65 ter 2792.1 will become Exhibit P2033. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, turning to paragraph 6 of your statement, you say in that paragraph: "I was not directly involved in the defence of Vukovar. However, we organised ourselves in the building where I lived." Can you please tell the Court what this organisation involved?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Well, how shall I explain? We, the residents of the building, organised ourselves to help the infirm, women and children, and cater to the needs of others in the building. That was outside the time that I spent doing my work obligation. That was in my free time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please elaborate on the types of activities that that organisation involved? You said that you helped the infirm, women, and children. Can you please describe exactly what that involved.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: A lot of residents of Vukovar rallied around. Not only those who were in the building, people who were living with their friends or family who had fled from buildings that had burned down from other areas. We had a lot of people to put up, to supply with food, water, electricity, to provide them with medical assistance, and other assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the activities you've just supplied, so supplying water, foods, and helping with the electricity and medical assistance, these relate to humanitarian activities. Were you at any point involved in any armed defence activities in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No, I did not participate in the armed conflict at all. All the activities I engaged in fell within the framework of my work obligation, of the company where I worked, and also in my building, where I lived. And that was my free choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, at paragraph 7 of your statement you say that your wife and yourself stayed in your apartment until 16th of November 1991 when that building burned down. Can you please describe for the Court what caused your building to burn down?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 16th of November, we lived in our own apartment. That day, in the early afternoon, the building was hit by a projectile from a gun or a mortar; I don't know exactly. And, as a result of that hit by a military projectile, the building was set on fire, and the whole building was seized by panic. Even a wall caved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you say that the building was hit by a projectile, what forces, what armed forces, hit your building with the projectile?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Well, those were -- I don't know whether I should call them the -- the enemy forces which attacked us and wanted to liberate Vukovar on their behalf. In any case, the projectile was launched from military weapons, according to what I know, from the direction of Negoslavci, which is in the east. And that's where the army was deployed with its heavy weaponry. That's where fire was opened from on Vukovar and that's where that projectile came, either from a cannon or a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Moving, then, to your time at the hospital in Vukovar, in your statement you say that you went there with your wife on the 19th of November, and you say that the situations in the hospital was very hard. Can you please describe for the Court the situation at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: The situation in the hospital was - how should I put it? - the hospital had already accommodated a lot of wounded and sick people. It functioned under very dire conditions in terms of the organisation, the staff, and the necessities that required to meet the conditions of life and work in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would now like to show you a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 4892.5, that's at tab 13 of the Court's bundle, be shown to the witness. And just to note, there is no transcripts for this video, and the Prosecution proposes only to rely on the footage in this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you recognise the scenes shown on this video?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised -- that video reflected the way patients were accommodated in the basement of the hospital. Everything that was above the basement on the ground floor was what was left of the building. All the patients were accommodated in the basement, in the corridors, and there was also a shelter that was connected to that basement area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 4892.5, be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd now like to show you another video that will appear before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 4892.6, that's again at tab 13 of the the Court's bundle, be shown. Again, there are no transcripts for the video. It's merely footage upon which the Prosecution wishes to rely.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you recognise the scenes depicted in the video that has just been shown?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. The last scene was the scene from that shelter which was part of the hospital basement. It also served to accommodate patients on the beds. There were a lot of them who -- whose beds were -- were in the corridors. Some of them did not even have beds.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 4892.6, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 14 of your statement, you describe how the soldiers separated women and children at the hospital. And later in your statement, you describe how you were ordered onto the buses in front of the hospital. What did you think would happen to you as you boarded the bus in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it happened, just the way you put it. However, we lived with a naive vision based on the information that the hospital would be evacuated into a neighbouring village called Sid on the border between Serbia and Croatia. And then from Sid we would be free to go wherever we wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I please now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 28 of your statement, you say that the five buses left the JNA barracks between 2.30 and 3.00 and headed towards Ovcara. I'd now like to show you a video-clip, and that will appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 5015.2 be shown and that's at tab 3 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you recognise the building that was shown in this video?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did you recognise the building to -- to be?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: That building was a storeroom or, rather, the place where agricultural machinery and equipment were stored. Those that belonged to the Vupik agricultural combine in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this the building in which you were detained along with other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, is this the building and the hangar near Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Well, what we saw in the clip were two hangars, both on the right-hand side. However the one that we were put in has a concrete path leading to the hangar from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 5015.2 be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 32 of your statement, you describe how you had to pass through a gauntlet and you were ordered inside the hangar to stand against the wall with the other prisoners. Before you reached that wall, you said that you were beaten by two Chetniks. Can you please describe for the Court what those men did to you.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Well, the buses arrived. You saw the road leading to the hangar in the video-clip. As buses arrived at the entrance into the hangar, they stopped and we had to get off one by one. We were met by two soldiers who searched us and who stole our property, to put it that way. They took all the valuables, including golden chains, rings, money, and similar things. I had a bag and in it I had clothes, some of which belonged to myself and the other -- to my wife and they took that away. They also took my coat and they took the documents that I had in my shirt pocket. I had my personal documents there and some money, and all those were taken by the two soldiers who met us as we get -- got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, at paragraph 32 of your statement you say that: "The whole process of entering the hangar took about an hour and it was about 4.00 when we all came in." Can you please describe for the Court the scene when all of the prisoners were inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: When all the detainees were inside in the hangar, I already said that in my statement, the principle of our arrival and accommodation along the walls of that hangar was that we faced the walls and our arms had to be above our heads. From the entrance to the hangar, on the right-hand side, around the hangar, in the shape of the Cyrillic letter P, the prisoners who were the last to arrive and who could no longer fit in the hangar because everything was already full on the -- along the walls of the hangar. On the opposite side of the hangar, there was a pile of straw. You know what straw is, don't you? And they were placed on that pile of straw, and they were in a more favourable position than us who had to face the hangar walls. They could sit on that pile of straw, and they could observe what was happening to us. It was rather calm. It was rather quiet. And all that time, there were regular soldiers of the JNA who were with us and who actually arranged us around that hangar. They were rather fair towards us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 33 of your statement, you describe an incident with a young JNA soldier who said to you: "You're surrounded by cold-blooded murders and you will be all killed tonight." Can you please tell the Court what went through your mind when you heard him say this to you?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. The young soldiers were very fair, but there were three of them who came behind my back with automatic rifles and they wanted me to give them money. They told me that if I had money and didn't give it to them, they would kill me. And finally one of them told me, "You would not need money anyway because we would all be killed that night." And what came to my mind at that moment I don't know. All sorts of things. And now after a such a long time, it's very difficult to remember what crossed my mind. But I'm sure that I had to be thinking about what will happen to me. What my lot would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at paragraph 38, you described how Mirko Ljubisic brought to you a JNA officer and said that you were not guilty. What did he mean when he said that you were not guilty?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: I never had a serious conversation with him about that event after the event. But what he meant was that I did not participate in the organisation of armed rebellion, I did not participate in armed conflict, and he thought that I had not sinned against anybody and I had not contributed to the situation that prevailed in Vukovar at the time, the situation of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we now please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd now like to move to your time at Velepromet. At paragraph 40 and 44 of your statement, you describe how you were taken from Ovcara to Velepromet and imprisoned in a room that you call the death room. Can you please tell the Court why you call that place the death room?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. That room was on the premises of Velepromet. It was a carpentry work-shop used by the company carpenters who repaired the equipment and maintained the building. But when it comes to the name "death room," that was mentioned in conversations amongst the prisoners. Those who were there before me, they told us that those who were taken from that room never returned, and that's why they were inspired to call it the death room.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'd like to show you one last document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 6440, that's at tab 18 of the Court's binder, be shown to the witness. Can I please ask that this not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature op this document?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell me why there are some names that have strikes next to their -- them, under paragraph 31 at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. Those are persons who were with me in the death room, and persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we didn't quite catch what you said. Can you please repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I said that those persons were with me in the death room, in the carpentry work-shop and who are no longer with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, just to make sure, Mr. Witness, are you -- what you just told us, is that with regard to the people that have a strike through the number before their names; that is, 2, 4, 5, 10, 14, and 15? Are those the people that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, under paragraph 32, in relation to Ovcara farm, you have -- there are circles next to a number of names over the course of the three pages. Can you please tell the Court why there are circles next to those names.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: The persons under 2 through 81 were killed at Ovcara. They all belonged to my group. They had all been taken from the hospital. I knew them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this 65 ter 6440 be admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2038, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones which are not in use please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I represent Goran Hadzic in these proceedings as his Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness be asked not to turn the pages so close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you kindly look at paragraph 5 in your statement where you stated that you had finally decided to give this statement after thinking long and hard. Could you tell me why did you have to think long and hard before giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: The period of war and everything that happened certainly left permanent consequences on all of us who survived it, especially those who survived specific events. The situation in Vukovar was very difficult and very unpleasant. Vukovar is a very idiosyncratic community that showed a face in the war that we hadn't known before. You used to be a friends with -- people with whom you socialised in cafes, at football matches, at work, suddenly became violent and threatened you. There were threats over the telephone. There were threats issued indirectly through third persons. There were people who could be suspected that they had been involved in something and could know something. There was also the consideration of my family. But, finally, I decided to give this statement and describe all that I've been through and all the events that I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further, in paragraph 26, you talk about a nurse who said to the medical staff that they should save their husbands, brothers, and sons because they were being taken to be executed. Could you just tell me where she said that? Where exactly. Because what is said here is that when five buses left the hospital, they headed for Ovcara. I understood the buses were headed to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes, first to the barracks and then to Ovcara. That is a nurse who worked at the medical centre who attended the briefing held in the surgical ward, in the plaster room specifically, where Sljivancanin made a speech, or, rather, delivered instructions to the medical staff as to how they should act if a time comes when patients need to be evacuated or saved. Now from whom she had heard this and why she said this, I don't know. I only learned from others that she told the medical staff that everybody who had been taken off by bus were taken to be executed. And if anybody has a family member amongst these people, they should try to save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us: Did she say this before the buses left the hospital; or did she say that after the buses had left? If you could be more precise.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I don't know this very precisely. But from all I know, I think she said that after the buses had left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you know to whom the nurse said this, do you know if those people listened to her? Did they try to do what she said?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes. One of them made a list of family members and people they knew from their own words, and she gave that list to Sljivancanin. And everybody on the list who had already been taken to the barracks were brought back, pursuant to Sljivancanin's orders. And all of them survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they were brought back, were they brought back from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I don't know whether you would move to another topic, but on this topic, I would like to ask the witness -- he told us that he only learned he had been taken off -- sorry. He only learned from others that she told the medical staff that everybody who had been taken off by bus were taken to be executed. My question, Mr. Witness, would be when did you hear that? When did you hear that she said this. Where were you when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago, so I can't tell you exactly. But that's what I learnt after leaving the camp, after the -- not after the interrogation and all the procedures, but it's either after I left the camp or after I was released from the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 31, you said, among other things, something about Slavko Dokmanovic. You said that he became involved very early on and he was very vociferous about promoting ideas about greater Serbia and that he was a very prominent person at public rallies organised by the Vukovar branch of the SDS. First of all, I would like to know if you can tell me: Did you attend any of those rallies organised by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear with your own ears his speeches promoting ideas about Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No. All I know, I know from people who were there and who listened to him and from press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he became involved very early on in promoting ideas about Greater Serbia, which period do you have in mind? Is it the period before the armed conflict in Croatia, in the spring and summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Most of all just before the beginning of the conflict. But he was known as an extremist. And he was also known as a football player, a professional in his own branch in Vukovar, and he was also seen going together with certain people to those rallies that were a harbinger of what was to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have information that at that time the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia was against the cessation of Croatia from Yugoslavia and against Croatian independence. Do you recall that? Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Not really because I was not involved in those things. I did not have any particular nationalist feelings, and I had also no contact with such persons who held their own closed meetings, preparing for certain missions, and preparing for the period that followed, so I would not be able to give you any specifics or any more detailed explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you lived in Vukovar, I suppose you knew a lot of people and you talked to a lot of people, you were able to hear what they thought. Are you aware that some people, especially among the Serbs, were against Croatia's cessation from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I've already told you, I did not get involved in such conversations and did not attend such rallies. But it was quite clear from the rallies in Serbia that the Serbs in Croatia, in the event of Croatia's cessation, were bent on keeping a part of Croatian territory and annexing it to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I know that from everyday life, from everything that went on, from minor and major incidents, public statements, et cetera. It was no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mention incidents, are you aware that people complained against incidents and attacks against Serbs and their property?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I didn't know anything specific in order to be able to confirm. But from the entire course of events, I know that such things happened on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to paragraph 33 of your statement. You said, among other things -- I'm not sure now if it's paragraph 33; at least that's what our LiveNote says. You said that before leaving the hangar, one man and you approached a Yugoslav officer saying that you were innocent. You had not done anything. Do you know anything about that officer? His rank?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I don't remember the details anymore. It was so many years ago, and I am getting on too. But that is the person who recognised me and took me out of the hangar. Before taking me out of the hangar, he took me to see that officer. I was rather dazed at the time, but I was surprised, I remember, that this officer wore his shirt unbuttoned, which was not really soldierly. And he had this ordinary cap on his head, not the usual officer's cap with a vizor. But that's all I can remember. I can't tell you anything more about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly the age of that officer? Was he your age, younger, older?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: He must have been younger because I was not young, even then. But it was rather dark in that hangar. I couldn't estimate his age. I don't know what the criteria were for promotion in the army and how many years of service you had to have for a certain rank. If I knew these things, then I could perhaps estimate his age. Also, if it had been lighter inside the hangar, maybe I could have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: When you left the hangar, did you notice any vehicles around?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: There were some passenger car, yes, parked on the side of the road. But these are all details that I cannot remember anymore. There were vehicles, but they were mostly passenger cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 61 in your statement. It is about your presence during the conversations, during the talks in Budapest in July 1992. Croatia was one of the participants, as well as Yugoslavia, and representatives of the Red Cross were also there. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you remember whether there were any words exchanged about Ovcara at that time?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I believe that that was the main topic, or, rather, the Vukovar Hospital was the main topic, because people who organised that meeting were mostly physicians and Dr. Bosanac as the head director of the hospital. And Ovcara and the events that took place there were also mentioned. And if you look at my statement, you will see that I talk about what was going on in the hospital, on the way from the hospital to Ovcara and back, and the final departure to Sremska Mitrovica, and everything that was said at the meeting was along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the position of Yugoslavia, i.e., what the Yugoslav side said about the destiny of the people who had been taken away from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: At that time, Ovcara was still a mystery. Nobody actually knew what had happened there. And the two sides, which were not that opposed to each other in those terms, one side tried to explain what had happened, and the other side accepted that with a lot of reservations, a lot of doubt as to what had happened. They did not believe the things happened the way they were described by the other side. Everything was within the framework of a polite exchange of thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. That was not discussed. However, that was the first such meeting for me. I attended the first such event that was supposed to reveal what had happened in the hospital and at Ovcara and the rest of the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, I would repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That would be good. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: According to what you know, was that the first such meeting between the two delegations or had there been other meetings that you did not attend? You already answered that, sir.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: I said I didn't know that. It was the first such meeting for me on that subject.

utterances.speaker: GH-054
utterances.text: But let's not waste time -- or, rather, we didn't want to waste time because we knew the same facts. I mostly confirmed what he said and added just a few details, mainly relative to what had happened to me and had not happened to this other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Dennehy, anything in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any re-direct. However, I would like to clarify one matter in the record, if I could. At page 10, line 19, there is a typographical error. It should read, as I tendered the exhibit, 4892.5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this brings your testimony to an end. You are released as a witness, and we thank you for coming to Zagreb to assist the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We should, indeed, continue with the next witness. I suppose we need Ms. Clanton in court now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We'll just reorganise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mujanovic. Is the next witness available?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The next witness is available. I just had to co-ordinate the two witnesses to be -- not to see each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So as soon as the next witness can be brought in, we will continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I just need one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, I would like to raise a procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yesterday I distributed a proofing note for this witness by e-mail and there were typos in this that were my mistakes and so I wanted to correct them now. The first one is in paragraph 3 of the proofing note. The last name that is listed in that paragraph, the first name of that person is incorrect. And the first name should be Mate. And in the last paragraph of the proofing note, the second-to-last line, the first name of the sister is incorrect. It should be Elizabeth. Those were my mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This is about the proofing -- Mr. Kovacevic's proofing note, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. This is for GH-138, Ms. Pitl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, it is for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Okay. And this is something you can correct and we don't have to ask the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to avoid any questions to the witness about this because as it was a mistake that I made and not her mistake. If possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's no objection from the Defence, it's on the record. Okay. Yes. Good morning, Madam Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I can, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Katarina Pitl is my name. I was born on the 27th of January, 1935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are about to make the solemn declaration, Madam Pitl, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth, and I must point out to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- by doing so you expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to this Tribunal. You understand? So would you now please read the solemn declaration the court usher gave to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Clanton, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Pitl.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, just so that you know, we will take a break for technical reasons as well as other reasons by 12.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. At -- well, let's take it on the safe side and we'll take the break in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, do you recall giving a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in November of 1998?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you recall that in October of 2012 --

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- you met with representatives of the Tribunal in Borovo Naselje to go over your statement again? Ms. Pitl, I'm going to ...

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't know that. I don't know that I met with somebody there. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, if we could please pull up 65 ter 6336. This is at tab 1, and it's a witness statement dated the 24th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, if you could look at the bottom right corner of the page that is page 4 in the B/C/S. This is page 1 of the English. At the bottom of page 4, do you recognise the signature? On the right.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. These are my initials on there; right? P and K.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, at page 4, do you see a signature?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Tell me what I'm supposed to say and I'll say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, I would like for you to look at the page that is the first page of this statement. It's page 4 of the B/C/S copy that is in front of you. And let me know when you have that in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, did you hear Mr. Mujanovic's question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I did not [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you repeat that, Mr. Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I was just requesting counsel to clarify whether she's referring to the attestation, which is in English in the copy I have, which is the first page of which the fourth page is the beginning, the first page of the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The question -- the question is whether -- can you read it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, it's not for you, Mr. Mujanovic. It's for Ms. Clanton who didn't hear you. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I cannot hear Mr. Mujanovic, but I was able to read the transcript. I think what he has asked is for the pages in the B/C/S and the English. And in the B/C/S, the cover page of the witness statement is page 4; and, in the English, it's page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does that clarify it for you, Mr. Mujanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We'll have to see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever I said, it was the truth. Please go on, put your questions, and I'll answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be all right if we take the break and get this sorted. I know we said in five minutes but I want to make sure that we're giving the correct pages. I have been told by the Registrar that this is page 7 in English, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that -- would that assist, Mr. Mujanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] If we make a break? Is that what you're suggesting, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. Whether the fact that this is page 7 in English, would that assist?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I don't think that would assist the witness because she is referring to the B/C/S version and she was looking at the cover page of the statement and her signature in [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I think the best option is to take the break and come back in half an hour and have this sorted out during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton -- sorry. Ms. Clanton, I think you can try to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. President, can I confirm that the witness is available? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness is there in front of us, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If I could please ask the Registrar to assist by providing you with 65 ter 6336. This is at tab 1. And if we could look at page 4 of the B/C/S version. Ms. Pitl, do you see a signature at the bottom right of this page?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Mine, Katarina Pitl.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, if the Registrar can assist you by turning to page 7 the B/C/S, please. Do you see a signature at the bottom right of this page?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And prior to testifying today, did you meet with representatives of the Tribunal to have your statement read back to you in your language?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And with respect to the statement in front of you, if you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this statement?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, the Prosecution would like to tender 65 ter 06336 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2039, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, for the record, please, what was the ethnicity of your husband?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: The same, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now the first topic I want to ask you about is what you observed in the summer of 1991. If I could ask for the Registrar's assistance, please. This is paragraph 5 of your statement. And it says that Erdut was shelled at the end of July 1991 by the JNA. It further says in paragraph 6 that you left Erdut on the 1st of August, 1991, and travelled to Aljmas in a van. I would like to know why you left your home in Erdut on this day.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Because we were under fire. The Serbs shot at us, and in my courtyard shrapnel was falling. A neighbour came. He said that shrapnel was also falling in his courtyard, not to leave the house. That was that. What were we supposed to do? Sit and wait?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could tell us what was different on the 1st of August from what you said earlier happened at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: I don't know. That was the beginning, and I heard early in the morning that there was shelling, that fire was opened. I was afraid that it might have been Borovo because that's where my children were. However, that was the police station in Dalj which was under attack. When I got up, I realised that it was in Dalj and that the -- the -- there were shots here in our village and that the military post was also attacked. My husband also got up and since our house was at the cross-roads in the centre of the village, he went to see what was going on. He said that the station was under attack and that was that. I don't know what you meant as the last thing. We went with the convoy. We joined the convoy and that's how we left Almas and went to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, what did you hear about groups near your home in Erdut or in the Dalj area?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: We were told that Arkan had crossed the bridge, that he was entering Erdut, and a neighbour -- or, rather, the neighbour's son came to us. His parents were in our basement. And he said that the entire village was in Aljmas, what are you waiting for. He loaded us onto a vehicle and we went with the hope that we would return. However, we never went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pitl. When you found out from the your neighbour that you had to leave, can you briefly tell us how you prepared to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: We didn't. We just left our house as we were. A small bag, the bare necessities, some -- a change of clothes, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about the cargo boat that you mention in paragraph 6 of your statement. This is the boat that you took from Aljmas to Osijek on the 1st of August, 1991. In your statement, in paragraph 6, it says that the roads out of Erdut were blocked and that there was panic. People trying to gather their families and leave Erdut as soon as possible. Further in that paragraph, you've said that the only way out of the area was by the river Danube. Can you describe the scene on the banks of the river Danube on that day?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when we arrived, there was complete chaos already on the bank of the Danube. You couldn't travel to Borovo, you couldn't travel to Osijek. The only way across the bridge was to Serbia, and they were not letting people cross the bridge. So everybody from the surrounding area gathered there. The only thing we could do was, coming from Aljmas, to jump into the Danube. There was so many people. Of course, I could not recognise all the people. There was already a crowd there. Many, many people. And that barge came from Osijek. It came, in fact, to pick up the wounded but eventually they took everyone on board and my husband put me on that barge. He said, "You have to go now," and -- and it was really lucky, fortunate, that I went.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the case manager to please pull up 65 ter number 06324.1. This is admitted Exhibit P94. This is a video-clip. For the record, it's an excerpt from V000-3844, and it goes from 16 seconds to 5 minutes and 5 seconds. And I would like for this to be played without the sound. There's no transcript to be tendered, and I would like to ask for this to be played to 1 minute and 6 seconds and then we will pause there. I should have said for the benefit of the Registrar that this is at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Pitl --

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- we've paused the video. Do you recognise the person in this still?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Of course I do. It's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And where are you standing at this time?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: It's before a house which housed a lot of displaced people in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what town is this in? Or village?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Aljmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, please, what day this video is taking place.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: The 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the case manager to please skip ahead to the 3-minute mark, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, we've paused the video again. I want to ask you: Were you part of the group that boarded this boat?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, could you repeat the answer to that question, please.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now, again, I would like to ask the case manager to please skip forward to 4 minutes and 38 seconds. And we're going to play from 4 minutes and 38 seconds to 5 minutes and 5 seconds, which is the end of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Pitl, in this video-clip that we watched, can you describe what the men on the shore are doing?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. They stayed behind and waved to us as we were departing. The barge departed and the people on the bank were waving to those of us they knew. Among them was my husband, but I can't identify him on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And other than what you've just mentioned in terms of the waving, can you tell us if the men on the shore were making any other gesture?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: With the leave of the President, I would like to ask to play that clip one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If the case manager could please go back to 4 minutes and 38 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well I can't recognise him. I don't know. He stayed behind, but I can't tell where he is. They told us to crouch because we were passing through an area where there was fighting in a nearby village, Bijelo Brdo. They wanted us to keep our heads low out of harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, can you describe for us -- and you have just said that you were keeping your head low and ducking to keep out of harm's way, what kind of harm did they think could happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The question was -- that asked was what harm did "they" think could happen. Clearly this witness is not in a position to know what "they" were thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you clarify what you mean by "they," Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to know what harm did you, Ms. Pitl, think could happen.

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: That they would be shooting from - how shall I put it? - from Bijelo Brdo. Bijelo Brdo was also again under their control. The Serbs' control. There was fighting there. They had surrounded Bijelo Brdo and Borovo, so there was no way to go except to go across the bridge which was also not possible. So we could only jump into the Danube. So when the barge headed towards Osijek we had go via Bijelo Brdo, and we had to crouch and keep our heads low, to duck, so that they wouldn't shoot at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, just to make this completely clear for the record. A moment ago you said "so that they wouldn't shoot at us." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Serbs. Well, the Serbs. Who else? Who else attacked us?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pitl. I'm now going to ask you a few questions about the fate of your husband, Franjo Pitl. When you gave your statement to the Tribunal in 1998, you said that you didn't know whether he was alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This is in paragraph 11 of her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you know today if he's alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. I know. I know because I went to identify the body, I recognised him. In fact, I recognised his suit, and he had two cheques for paying rent and electricity in his pockets, and they asked me what he was wearing when he was taken away. I didn't know because I wasn't there, but when I saw him, I saw that those were his clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, and this is in paragraphs 7 and 8, you've described what you were told by others about what happened to your husband after he returned to Erdut. My question is: Did you hear that any other persons from Erdut disappeared during the same time-period?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes, I heard. I heard from a couple of women I knew who were there at the time when he was taken away, but I know about all the other people who were taken away at the same time as he was, and he was -- they were buried at the same place they were executed. Thrown into the Danube. Some were found in a well in the area of Dalj, Daljski Atar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, you've told us that you know about all the other people who were taken away at the same time as he was. Do you recall any of their names?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. Stevo Tesanac, then what's his last name? You know it's been 20, 22 years. Franjo's niece, Jelica of the Alberts. Her husband. Her sister-in-law. I can't remember everybody's name because I haven't lived in Erdut for a long time. There were quite a few people I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to call up 65 ter 06448. This is the document that was provided by the witness during proofing. We sent it through yesterday. It's at tab 7 of the revised exhibit list. And the Defence has indicated they have no objection, so we would ask that it be added to the 65 ter list and also available to the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Of course, I do. Not each and every one of them, but they're all from Erdut, and I know quite a lot of people on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us the Chamber who do you know that is pictured there?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, my Franjo. Franjo Pitl. Andreja Matin. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, I can clarify my question for you. Of the people that you see there, can you tell us which people are people that you know, of course, in addition to your late husband?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. I know Andrija Matin. I know Matej Butkovic, Jelica Albert and her Djuro. Viktorija Albert. Manda Maj, Stevo Tesanac and this Ana Terzic. I don't know the rest. But there are not many left; two or three.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, a moment ago you mentioned Andrija Matin. I want to ask you, what did you hear about Andrija Matin related to the day of your husband's disappearance?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: I heard that Andrija was already in a tractor trailer when three men came to round up Franjo. He was already sitting on a trailer. There was one woman, Stana, who is now dead. She was passing through my house. She had gone to the bakers to buy some bread and she happened to pass by just as this was happening. She's the one who told me. Unfortunately, she died. It's quite a long time ago. She's no longer with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, the persons that you identified as people that you knew who were on the document in front of you, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would seek to tender 06448 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2040, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Pitl, I just have one more topic that I want to cover with you. What I want to ask you is other than the disappearances and the killings that you've -- excuse me. Other than the disappearances and the persons who you've identified on the document in front of you, I would like to know if you know what happened to other Croats who stayed in Erdut after you left on August 1st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, elderly people remained, at least some of them; let's say, enough to fill a bus. And they were sent to Osijek on a bus towards the very end. They were the only ones who stayed behind in Erdut. And, later on, they were transported to Osijek. They were also Croats. And no other Croats remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Pitl, you just described persons who were sent to Osijek on a bus. Can you tell me who sent them?

utterances.speaker: KATARINA PITL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, those Serbs who came into Erdut and who rounded up and killed our younger men. But they didn't kill the older ones. Instead, they sent them to Osijek, to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pitl, this brings your testimony to an end. Thank you for assisting the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you too. I wish you all the best. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We have one hour left. Mr. Kovacevic is in the building. We are at a cross-examination exercise, right? Are you ready, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll do some reorganisation so Mr. Gillett can come into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And can we bring the witness in, in the meantime, or should we ask -- should we wait for Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think it's okay to bring the witness in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic. Please be seated. Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning -- or good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you crossed over the bridge or -- sorry, that you crossed over the river Danube in a ferry and that this was 1 or 2 kilometres from the bridge itself. Do you remember as you're facing the bridge from Serbia crossing to Croatia were you to the right of the bridge or to the left of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right of the bridge, looking from Serbia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that upstream or downstream from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Downstream.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we left off, we were discussing your trip to Pacetin. And am I correct in understanding that between -- while travelling between Vera and Pacetin, you would pass through the town of Bobota?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not going from Vera to Pacetin via Bobota. I said we took the dirt road through the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you say you didn't pass through Bobota?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there some reason why you couldn't take the road that connected Vera and Bobota, the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was, was that there was frequent shooting at the road going from Vera to Pacetin and Brsadin and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, let's focus right now on my question. The connection, the road between Vera and Bobota. Are you saying that the road between Vera and Bobota was not safely passable at the time that you were making this journey?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's have 1D444, please. This is Defence tab 30. And while that's coming up, where was the firing that endangered the road between Vera and Bobota? And by "firing," I mean rifle fire, artillery fire, mortar fire. Any kind of danger. Where was that originating from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire came from a place called Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a little bit on this. That's good. Maybe just slightly move the image downwards. I mean up. That's perfect right there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, am I correct, sir, that -- can you see Bobota there on this image, marked on this image?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this image, I can't see -- could you please bear with me for a moment. Yes, I can see Bobota above Pacetin. And you -- you can also see Trpinja, a place on the northern side in the direction of Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we see a road heading north from Bobota. Am I correct in saying that if you follow that road a little ways and, unfortunately, it's not visible on this image, but if you follow that road a little ways to the north, you reach Vera; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the road marked as 2 from Trpinja to Vera. And there's another one from Pacetin via Bobota, but it's not marked here by any numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Correct, it's not marked by any numbers. But if you look there at the screen, you do see what appears to be a road marked in yellow; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if you follow that road north from Bobota, you reach Vera; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How far is that, from Bobota to Vera?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the distance in kilometres. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you were a driver. That was your job. How do you not know the distance in kilometres between Vera and Bobota?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1991. I can't remember. But it can't be more than 10 to 15 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that it's about the same distance as between Bobota and Pacetin? Or is it more, or is it less? Just give us an idea. It doesn't have to be perfect.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the distance from Bobota to Vera is slightly more than from there to Pacetin. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Down there at the bottom of the screen, do you see Nustar, apparently, marked?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nustar is marked by an inscription. It was on the road marked by number 55, the road that led from Nustar towards Brsadin and further on towards Borovo Naselje. And on the other side, it went in the direction of Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's the location from which you say there was fire -- or there was artillery based that made it unsafe for you to travel on the asphalt road not only between Bobota and Pacetin, but between Vera and Bobota; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was not safe to travel from Pacetin along the road that joined the road number 55 leading towards Brsadin. We used the dirt road between Pacetin and Trpinja road in the direction of the Brsadin silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the dirt road is no further from the source of the fire than is the asphalt road. Is that a correct statement or is that not a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the road was a little bit further than the asphalt road. However, nobody opened fire on those dirt roads, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
